docs.title: Machine Learning for Materials Discovery
docs.text:
Materials discovery has entered a data-driven era. Synthesising novel compounds by trial and error takes months in the laboratory. Chemical space is vast. In contrast, computational screening evaluates thousands of formulations in seconds.

Machine learning enables this acceleration. By converting chemical formulae into composition-based physical descriptors1112, statistical models capture complex structure-property relationships. These descriptors summarise properties such as atomic radii, electronegativities, valence electron counts and melting temperatures. They require no expensive quantum mechanical calculations.

Here I present three interactive tools that I built for functional materials discovery. The first two target high-entropy alloy superconductors. The third focuses on porous carbon supercapacitor electrodes. Each tool combines predictive modelling with physical constraints to guide laboratory synthesis.

docs.title: High-Entropy Superconductor Tc Prediction
docs.text: Two-stage machine learning pipeline coupling phase stability classification with critical temperature regression.

docs.title: Why the Problem Matters
docs.text:
High-entropy alloys (HEAs) mix 4 to 6 principal metallic elements in near-equimolar proportions5. This composition strategy creates vast combinatorial spaces with unexpected functional behaviours. In 2014, Koželj and co-workers reported the first superconducting HEA: Ta-Nb-Hf-Zr-Ti2. It forms a body-centred cubic (BCC) solid solution with a superconducting transition temperature (Tc) of about 7.3 K2. Conventional electron-phonon coupling in these alloys follows BCS theory1. Empirically, Tc correlates with the valence electron concentration (VEC)43.

Most known superconducting HEAs adopt a single-phase BCC crystal structure, though other phases exist3. Identifying new high-entropy superconductors (HES) requires answering two distinct questions. First, will a given mixture of elements form a single-phase solid solution? Second, what is its critical temperature? Most machine learning models predict Tc while ignoring phase formation altogether. Synthesising an alloy that segregates into brittle intermetallics wastes experimental time. I built a two-stage machine learning pipeline that addresses both stability and superconductivity.

docs.title: How the Pipeline Works
docs.text:
I split the prediction task into two sequential stages:

  1. Stage 1: Phase stability classifier. An alloy must first form a stable BCC phase. I trained an Extra Trees classifier13 on 11,247 experimentally observed HEA compositions compiled by Peivaste et al.9. The model predicts six distinct phase categories: BCC, FCC, BCC+FCC, intermetallic, amorphous, and mixed. It builds upon previous data-driven phase prediction methodologies10. The model achieves 96% accuracy for BCC identification and 83% accuracy across all six categories.
  2. Stage 2: Critical temperature regression. Once an alloy passes the BCC phase gate, six regression models predict Tc: Extra Trees, Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, XGBoost, Support Vector Regression (SVR), and K-Nearest Neighbours (KNN). I featurised each alloy using 138 Magpie composition descriptors via the matminer library1112. The training set comprises 3,319 superconductors: 3,253 metallic entries from the SuperCon database and 66 high-entropy alloys. This approach builds on earlier machine learning studies on the SuperCon repository67.

docs.title: Model Performance and Validation
docs.text:
The six regression models perform consistently under cross-validation. Extra Trees and Random Forest delivered the highest accuracy.

Model Cross-Validation MAE (K) Cross-Validation R² Extra Trees 0.84 0.87 Random Forest 0.93 0.87 XGBoost 1.04 0.86 K-Nearest Neighbours (KNN) 1.03 0.83 Support Vector Regression (SVR) 1.21 0.81 Gradient Boosting 1.36 0.81

Feature importance analysis reveals clear physical drivers. The most important descriptors are the range of elemental melting temperatures and the most common elemental space group. Both relate to interatomic bonding and crystal structure.

As a sanity check, I tested the benchmark NbTaTiZrHf alloy2. My Extra Trees model predicts a Tc of about 6.8 K. This prediction aligns well with the experimental value of about 7.3 K.

docs.title: Limits and Operational Bounds
docs.text:
Critical Assumptions and Limitations

  • Limited HEA Training Data: Only 66 of the 3,319 training samples are high-entropy alloys. The remaining samples are conventional binary and ternary metallic superconductors. Predictive accuracy on unexplored HEA families is likely lower than cross-validation metrics indicate.
  • Extrapolation Overestimation: Random cross-validation on the SuperCon database overestimates model performance when extrapolating to new chemical classes8.
  • Absence of Negative Superconductivity Labels: The regression models were trained exclusively on known superconductors. The algorithms always return a positive Tc. They cannot recognise when an alloy fails to superconduct. For example, the non-superconducting CoCrFeNiMn Cantor alloy produces a false prediction of about 4.7 K.
  • Magnetic Element Suppression: Ferromagnetic and 3d transition elements (Fe, Co, Ni, Mn) break Cooper pairs and strongly suppress superconductivity. Compositions rich in these elements should be interpreted with extreme caution.
  • Phase Gate Validity Domain: The Stage 1 phase classifier applies strictly to high-entropy alloys containing 4 to 6 elements, with each element present at 5 to 35 atomic percent.

docs.title: How to Use the Tool
docs.text:
Enter any multi-component alloy formula into the web interface. The tool verifies that the formula falls within the 4 to 6 element domain. It runs Stage 1 to estimate P(BCC), then Stage 2 predicts Tc with all six models. Out-of-domain inputs, non-BCC phases and magnetic-element-rich compositions are clearly flagged. The tool shows the selected model's Tc with its ± MAE and the spread across all six models.

→ Tc Prediction Tool

docs.title: Inverse Design: HES Compositions for a Target Tc
docs.text: Inverse design screening pipeline evaluating 672 refractory alloy candidates through physical gates.

docs.title: Why the Problem Matters
docs.text: Forward regression answers: "What is the Tc of this alloy?" Experimental researchers face the reverse challenge: "Which elemental compositions should I synthesise to reach a target Tc?" Testing candidate mixtures one by one in an arc furnace is slow. Inverse design and active learning systematically screen large compositional libraries to discover optimal candidates14.

docs.title: How the Pipeline Works
docs.text:
I designed an inverse screening workflow tailored to refractory high-entropy alloys:

  1. Candidate Enumeration: I enumerated all equimolar 4, 5, and 6 element combinations drawn from 10 refractory metals (Nb, Ta, Ti, Zr, Hf, V, Mo, W, Re, Ru). This combinatorial pool yields 672 unique candidate alloys.
  2. Phase Stability Gate: The Stage 1 Extra Trees classifier screens all 672 formulations. The system retains only candidates with P(BCC) ≥ 0.7. This step eliminates combinations prone to phase separation or multiphase intermetallics.
  3. Multi-Model Tc Prediction: All six regression models predict Tc independently for each surviving BCC candidate.
  4. 5-Check Verification Gate: To filter out model artefacts, each candidate must pass five heuristic checks:
    • Phase Stability: P(BCC) ≥ user threshold (default 0.7).
    • Cross-Model Agreement: The standard deviation of the six model predictions is at most 2.0 K.
    • Physical Bounds: The ensemble mean Tc falls inside the designated search window.
    • Valence Electron Count: The valence electron concentration (VEC) falls in the viable superconducting range of 3.5 to 7.543.
    • Novelty: The composition is not already in the training data (it may still be known in the literature).
  5. Composite Scoring and Ranking: Surviving alloys are evaluated using a composite objective function. The score balances proximity to the target Tc, phase stability confidence, and inter-model consensus.

The workflow returns the top-ranked candidates that pass every check. Each candidate is scored with the full six-model ensemble, so screening is compute-heavy. On the current free cloud server, each candidate takes about 13 s, so the online tool screens a chosen element pool of up to 20 candidates (about 4 minutes). The full 672-alloy screen is best run offline.

docs.title: Experimental Context and Limitations
docs.text:
Computational Hypotheses, Not Guaranteed Discoveries

Inverse design candidate lists are prioritised hypotheses for laboratory experimentation. They are not guaranteed physical discoveries. The same data and domain limitations described in Section 1 apply directly to these predictions. High predicted Tc values must always be confirmed through vacuum arc melting, phase characterisation via X-ray diffraction, and low-temperature resistivity or magnetometry measurements.

docs.title: How to Use the Tool
docs.text:
Choose a target Tc, an element pool and the alloy sizes to screen, then set the acceptance thresholds. The tool shows how many candidates that implies and roughly how long it will take. Results list each composition with its ensemble Tc, model spread, 95% interval, P(BCC), VEC and which checks it passed. Candidates are screened hypotheses, not confirmed superconductors.

→ Inverse Design Tool

docs.title: Carbon Supercapacitor Inverse Design
docs.text: Physics-informed Gaussian process regression and Bayesian optimisation loop for porous carbon electrodes.

docs.title: Why the Problem Matters
docs.text:
Electrochemical double-layer capacitors (EDLCs) provide high power density and rapid charge-discharge capability. They store energy electrostatically via ion electrosorption at the electrode-electrolyte interface1921. Capacitance scales primarily with accessible specific surface area (SSA)1921. However, sub-nanometre pores under 1 nm dramatically boost area-normalised capacitance by forcing partial desolvation of electrolyte ions20.

Synthesising porous carbon requires balancing surface area, pore size distribution, heteroatom doping, and current density. Traditional synthesis involves extensive empirical optimisation. To accelerate this search, I developed a physics-informed machine learning and Bayesian optimisation system. It predicts specific capacitance and solves the inverse problem: identifying synthesis targets for a desired capacitive performance.

docs.title: Forward Model: Physics-Informed GPR
docs.text:
I constructed a forward surrogate using Gaussian process regression (GPR)15. I engineered a custom kernel that encodes a physical monotonicity prior: specific capacitance grows monotonically with accessible surface area, consistent with the Gouy-Chapman-Stern electric double-layer model21. The GPR framework provides calibrated predictive uncertainties alongside point predictions.

To benchmark the Gaussian process, I also trained a Gradient Boosting regressor. I analysed this benchmark using Tree-SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations)18 to verify that learned feature importances reflect established electrochemistry.

I also engineered seven physics-derived features grounded in EDLC theory: micropore fraction (micropore area divided by total surface area), a pore density proxy, an SSA-nitrogen synergy term, total heteroatom content (nitrogen plus oxygen), a defect-surface coupling term, the square of the voltage window (stored energy scales with V2), and a rate penalty for high current density.

docs.title: Inverse Design via Bayesian Optimisation
docs.text:
The trained GPR serves as the surrogate model in a Bayesian optimisation loop17. Given a target specific capacitance, the algorithm navigates the multidimensional parameter space using the Expected Improvement (EI) acquisition function16. The optimisation operates under explicit physical constraints: - Micropore surface area cannot exceed total surface area (SSA_micro ≤ SSA). - Pore size must be at least 0.3 nm, roughly the size of a bare electrolyte ion.

The algorithm samples the acquisition function to recommend optimal electrode parameters in real time.

docs.title: Dataset and Offline Metrics
docs.text:
I trained and evaluated the models on a curated dataset of 558 carbon electrode entries compiled from literature.

Model Offline R² RMSE (F/g) 95% Interval Coverage Physics-Informed GPR 0.50 73 95.5% Gradient Boosting Benchmark 0.57 68 N/A

The model achieves moderate predictive accuracy. This performance reflects the modest sample size (558 entries) and substantial variations in experimental protocols across literature sources (three-electrode versus two-electrode cells, differing electrolytes, and varying mass loadings). Importantly, the physics-informed GPR achieves 95.5% coverage on its 95% prediction intervals, demonstrating well-calibrated uncertainty.

docs.title: Operational Reality and Active Development
docs.text:
Current Deployed Model Limitations

In live testing of the currently deployed web tool, predictions respond only to total specific surface area. None of the other inputs currently change the output. Typical uncertainty is about ±109 F/g on predictions near 200 F/g. The deployed surrogate therefore needs retraining so that all descriptors contribute, as they did in the offline model. The interactive tool states this limitation clearly.

docs.title: Related Experimental Work
docs.text: This machine learning pipeline complements my experimental background in capacitive energy storage. For details on my laboratory synthesis of hybrid reduced graphene oxide and transition metal oxide materials, see my MSc hybrid rGO, Ni(OH)2, MnO2 electrodes article.

docs.title: How to Use the Tool
docs.text:
For forward prediction, set the electrode descriptors and read the predicted capacitance with its uncertainty. For inverse design, enter a target capacitance and choose the electrolyte, test method and carbon type. Bayesian optimisation then returns candidate electrode parameters with their predicted capacitance and uncertainty. While the deployed model depends only on surface area, treat the other suggested parameters as unoptimised.

→ Supercapacitor Design Tool

docs.title: What I Learned and Next Steps
docs.text:
Building these machine learning tools highlighted three valuable lessons:

  1. Domain knowledge must guide algorithms. Machine learning models trained purely on composition can output unphysical results. Enforcing phase stability filters and physics-informed covariance kernels prevents algorithms from making impossible recommendations.
  2. Uncertainty quantification is vital for materials synthesis. A point prediction without an error bar provides little guidance in the laboratory. Reporting prediction intervals and inter-model variances allows researchers to gauge risk before synthesising new materials.
  3. Data quality limits extrapolation. Curating clean, standardised training data remains the central bottleneck in materials informatics. Literature datasets vary widely in testing protocols and reporting standards.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text: The clearest improvements are: more high-entropy alloy training data, including alloys that do not superconduct, so the model can learn when superconductivity is absent; a deployed supercapacitor surrogate in which every descriptor contributes; and an active learning loop that feeds new experimental results back into training14.

docs.title: Research
docs.text: I study how processing and composition control the properties of functional materials. My current focus is magnetic and superconducting materials, guided by machine learning.

docs.title: Research interests
docs.text:
• Permanent magnets: NdFeB magnets, from design to working prototype.
  • Superconductors: ductile high-entropy superconductors for fusion, and MgB2 joints for MRI magnets.
  • Energy storage: supercapacitor electrodes and related nanomaterials.
  • Machine learning for materials: property prediction and inverse design. See Machine Learning.

NdFeB magnets are the strongest permanent magnets in use today. I am developing an NdFeB based magnet, from initial design through to a working prototype. The work relates processing route and composition to magnetic performance.

docs.text:
The University of Queensland · 2026 – present

Fusion magnets need superconductors that can be shaped into wire without cracking. I am developing a ductile superconductor based on high-entropy alloys for this purpose. Machine learning guides which compositions to make, using the prediction and inverse design tools I built.

Read about high-entropy superconductors in my blog →

docs.title: MgB₂ reacted joints for persistent-mode MRI magnets
docs.text:
The University of Queensland · 2022 – 2026

An MRI magnet in persistent mode holds a stable field without a power supply. This requires superconducting joints with extremely low resistance. My PhD developed a fabrication method for reacted MgB2 joints for industrial MRI magnets.

I synthesised the MgB2 myself and formed each joint with a specialised process. Joint performance was validated by its transport critical current (Ic).

Industry funded and under IP protection. Publications are on hold pending patent clearance.

Read about MgB₂ joints in my blog →

Bangladesh University of Engineering and Technology

I developed a ternary hybrid electrode of Ni(OH)2, MnO2 and reduced graphene oxide (rGO). Its wrinkled, flower-like structure improved charge storage. The work was published in ACS Omega.

docs.title: High-entropy superconductors: order from chemical chaos
docs.text: Metallurgy has long followed a simple recipe: take one main metal and add small amounts of others. High-entropy alloys break that rule. They mix five or more elements in near-equal amounts, and some of them superconduct. They may help solve one of fusion energy's hardest materials problems.

docs.title: Superconductivity in one minute
docs.text:
Below a critical temperature, Tc, some materials lose all electrical resistance. Electrons pair up into Cooper pairs, bound together through vibrations of the crystal lattice. The pairs then move through the material without scattering.1

On cooling, resistance falls gradually, then drops to exactly zero at Tc.

Zero resistance means a coil can carry a huge current without heating. That is why superconducting magnets produce fields far stronger than ordinary electromagnets.

docs.title: The fusion magnet problem
docs.text:
A tokamak confines plasma hotter than the Sun's core inside a ring of magnetic field. The magnets must carry enormous currents in high fields, survive huge mechanical forces, and work for decades.

ITER, the international fusion experiment in France, shows the scale. Its magnet system uses 18 toroidal field coils and a central solenoid wound from Nb3Sn, plus poloidal field coils wound from Nb–Ti.2 All use cable-in-conduit conductors: hundreds of superconducting strands twisted into a cable and sealed inside a steel jacket, with helium flowing through to cool them.2

Today's conductor choices each involve a trade-off:

Conductor Tc Mechanical behaviour Fusion use Nb–Ti about 9 K Ductile alloy; easy to draw into wire Lower-field coils (ITER poloidal field) Nb3Sn about 18 K Brittle intermetallic; strain sensitive High-field coils (ITER toroidal field, central solenoid) REBCO (high-temperature superconductor) about 90 K Thin ceramic layer on a metal tape Compact high-field tokamaks Ta–Nb–Hf–Zr–Ti (high-entropy alloy) about 7 K Metallic BCC alloy Research stage

Values from Larbalestier et al.,3 Godeke4 and Koželj et al.5

Nb3Sn performs well at high field, but it is so brittle that coils are usually wound first and reacted afterwards ("wind and react").4 High-temperature superconductors are advancing fast. In 2021, a large REBCO test coil for the SPARC tokamak reached a peak field of about 20 T.6 Even so, a conductor combining Nb–Ti's ductility with better superconducting performance would be valuable. This is where high-entropy alloys come in.

docs.title: What is a high-entropy alloy?
docs.text:
In 2004, two groups independently explored alloys made of many principal elements in equal proportions.78 Intuition suggested such mixtures would form many brittle phases. Instead, some formed a single, simple crystal structure.

Five elements share one body-centred cubic (BCC) lattice, with each site occupied at random.

The name comes from configurational entropy. For n elements in equal amounts, the mixing entropy is

ΔSconf = R ln n

where R is the gas constant. For five elements this is about 1.61 R. At high temperature, this entropy term can stabilise a random solid solution over competing ordered phases.7

docs.title: Superconducting high-entropy alloys
docs.text:
In 2014, Koželj and colleagues reported the first superconducting high-entropy alloy: Ta–Nb–Hf–Zr–Ti, with a BCC structure and a Tc of about 7.3 K.5 Later work showed its zero resistance survives pressures up to 190 GPa, a remarkable robustness.9

Since then, many related alloys have been studied.10 Their Tc follows trends with the average number of valence electrons per atom. This echoes an empirical rule first noted by Matthias in the 1950s.11 Three design questions now drive the field:

  1. Can Tc and the upper critical field be raised while keeping a single BCC phase?
  2. Does chemical disorder help pin magnetic flux, which sets how much current a wire can carry in a field?
  3. Can the alloy stay ductile enough to be drawn into fine filaments?

docs.title: How superconducting wire is made today
docs.text:
A practical fusion conductor is not a single wire. It is a composite of many fine superconducting filaments in a copper matrix. The copper carries current safely if the superconductor briefly fails, and it conducts heat away.

The conventional route for multifilamentary superconducting wire and fusion coils.

For a ductile alloy such as Nb–Ti, the route looks like this:34

  1. Alloy melting. The alloy is melted, typically by vacuum arc or electron-beam melting, to get a clean, homogeneous ingot.
  2. Homogenisation. A long heat treatment evens out the composition.
  3. Rod making. The ingot is worked into rods and clad in copper.
  4. Billet assembly. Thousands of hexagonal copper-clad rods are stacked inside a copper can.
  5. Hot extrusion. The billet is pushed through a die, bonding everything into one composite.
  6. Wire drawing. The composite is drawn down through many dies. Intermediate heat treatments create nanoscale precipitates that pin magnetic flux.3
  7. Cabling. Strands are twisted into a cable, then jacketed (cable-in-conduit).
  8. Coil winding. The cable is wound into the final coil.

Brittle Nb3Sn needs a different trick. Its precursors (niobium and tin, or bronze) are drawn while still ductile. The compound forms only in a final reaction heat treatment, usually after the coil is wound.4 A ductile superconducting high-entropy alloy could follow the simpler Nb–Ti route, with no reaction step.

docs.text:

How Nb3Sn and Nb–Ti superconducting wires are manufactured (Professor Harry Bhadeshia, University of Cambridge channel).

An introduction to high-entropy alloys by materials scientist Taylor Sparks.

docs.title: Who makes fusion superconductors?
docs.text: Superconducting strand is a specialised industry. For ITER's toroidal field coils alone, suppliers across six ITER members (China, Europe, Japan, Korea, Russia and the United States) produced more than 400 tonnes of Nb3Sn strand.12 Europe's share was made by Bruker EAS in Germany and Oxford Superconducting Technology (OST) in the United States, using the bronze and internal-tin routes respectively.13

docs.title: Searching a huge composition space
docs.text:
With ten candidate metals and freedom over proportions, the number of possible alloys is enormous. Making and testing each one is not practical. Machine learning helps narrow the search. Composition-based descriptors, such as averaged elemental properties, allow a model to learn from known alloys.14

I built a two-stage approach. First, a classifier predicts whether a composition forms a stable single-phase BCC structure. Second, a set of regression models predicts Tc for the compositions that pass. You can try both on my Machine Learning page.

docs.title: My work
docs.text:
At The University of Queensland, I am developing a ductile superconductor based on high-entropy alloys for fusion applications. Machine learning guides which compositions to synthesise. Experiments then test both the superconducting properties and the mechanical behaviour that wire manufacturing requires.

The big picture

High-entropy alloys turn chemical disorder into a design tool. For superconductors, the goal is a conductor that is both strong in high fields and easy to manufacture.

docs.title: Closing the loop: MgB₂ superconducting joints for MRI
docs.text: An MRI scanner holds an extremely stable magnetic field for years, with its power supply switched off. That trick depends on a few tiny connections inside the magnet: the superconducting joints. My PhD focused on making those joints from a promising superconductor, magnesium diboride.

docs.title: How an MRI magnet stays on
docs.text:
Most clinical MRI magnets are wound from niobium–titanium (Nb–Ti) wire and cooled in liquid helium to about 4.2 K.1 Once the coil is energised, the circuit is closed with a superconducting switch. The power supply is then disconnected. Current keeps circulating with no driving voltage. This is called persistent mode.

The field is only as stable as the loop is perfect. Any residual resistance R in the circuit makes the current decay with a time constant

τ = LR

where L is the coil inductance.2 MRI needs field drift measured in parts per million over long periods. So the total resistance must be vanishingly small.1

With a superconducting joint the field stays flat; any resistance makes it decay over time.

The wire itself is superconducting. The weak points are the joints, where separate lengths of wire must be connected. A large magnet contains many coil sections, a persistent switch and leads, so it needs several joints. Every one must be superconducting.2

docs.title: Why magnesium diboride?
docs.text:
In 2001, Nagamatsu and colleagues discovered that MgB2, a simple and inexpensive compound, superconducts at 39 K.3

MgB2 stacks graphite-like boron layers between layers of magnesium. Vibrations of the boron layers drive its superconductivity. Nb–Ti MgB2 Critical temperature about 9 K 39 K Typical operating temperature in MRI 4.2 K (liquid helium bath) about 10 to 20 K (cryocooler) Raw materials Niobium, titanium Magnesium, boron (abundant, low cost) Mechanical behaviour Ductile alloy Brittle ceramic-like compound

Sources: Larbalestier et al.,4 Buzea and Yamashita,5 and Parizh et al.6

This higher Tc matters for MRI. MgB2 magnets can run cooled by cryocoolers, without a large liquid helium bath.6 Helium is a finite and increasingly costly resource, so reducing dependence on it is attractive. Some designs go further and use a frozen solid cryogen as a thermal buffer, keeping the magnet cold through power cuts.7

docs.title: How MgB₂ wire is made
docs.text:
MgB2 is too brittle to draw on its own. Instead, manufacturers use the powder-in-tube (PIT) method: powder is sealed inside a metal tube and the whole composite is drawn into wire.8

The conventional powder-in-tube route for MgB2 wire and coils.
  1. Powder preparation. In the in situ route, magnesium and boron powders are mixed (Mg + 2B). In the ex situ route, ready-made MgB2 powder is used.8
  2. Tube filling. The powder is packed into a metal tube. A barrier layer, often niobium or iron, stops magnesium reacting with the outer sheath.
  3. Drawing and rolling. The tube is reduced through dies and grooved rolls.
  4. Restacking. Several mono-filament wires are bundled into a new tube to make a multifilament conductor.
  5. Final drawing. The composite is drawn to its final diameter.
  6. Reaction heat treatment. In the in situ route, heating under argon converts Mg + 2B into MgB2 inside the wire.
  7. Coil winding. The wire is wound into coils, either before the reaction ("wind and react") or after it ("react and wind").9
  8. Joints and magnet assembly. Coils, switch and leads are joined into one superconducting circuit.

The in situ reaction shrinks in volume, leaving pores that block current. To get denser superconductor, internal magnesium infiltration places a magnesium rod at the centre of a boron layer. On heating, the magnesium infiltrates the boron and forms a dense MgB2 layer.10

docs.title: Who makes MgB₂ conductors?
docs.text:
A small number of companies produce MgB2 wire commercially. ASG Superconductors in Genoa, Italy, makes long-length PIT wire. It has built a 0.5 T, cryogen-free open MRI scanner wound with MgB2.1112 In the United States, Hyper Tech Research develops wire made by internal magnesium infiltration.10

ASG Superconductors: developing MgB2 wire, from powder synthesis to the final stage.

Inside ASG Superconductors' MgB2 wire production facility.

docs.title: Why MgB₂ joints are hard
docs.text:
Joining MgB2 is much harder than joining Nb–Ti, for several reasons:65

  • It is brittle. MgB2 cannot be welded or crimped like a ductile metal.
  • Magnesium is reactive and volatile. Forming dense, well-connected MgB2 at the joint, rather than in a controlled wire, is difficult.
  • The wire is a composite. Filaments sit inside metal sheaths and barriers. These must be opened and the superconducting cores connected without damaging them.
  • Grain connectivity is critical. Current must pass through continuous, well-connected grains. Porosity and impurity phases block it.

Researchers have pursued several strategies, and joints with very low resistance have been reported.13 Joints made from already reacted wire are especially challenging. The superconductor has formed before joining, so the joint must create a new superconducting path between two finished conductors.

docs.title: How a joint is judged
docs.text: The decisive test is the transport critical current, Ic. A current is passed through the joint at a set temperature and magnetic field. Ic is the current at which resistance first appears. A good joint carries a current comparable to the wire itself, under the conditions the magnet will see. Long-term persistent-mode tests then measure any slow field decay directly.

docs.title: My work
docs.text:
During my PhD at The University of Queensland, I developed a method for joining reacted MgB2 for persistent-mode MRI magnets. The aim was ultra-low joint resistance for stable circulating current and long-term field stability. The work combined synthesis, heat treatment, microscopy and low-temperature transport measurements.

Industry funded · IP protected

This project is industry funded, and its methods are under intellectual-property protection. Details and publications will follow once patent clearance allows.

docs.title: NdFeB magnets: the small giants behind modern motors
docs.text: Every electric car, wind turbine and smartphone vibration motor relies on a magnet you have probably never seen. It is made of neodymium, iron and boron. Gram for gram, it is the strongest permanent magnet ever commercialised.

docs.title: A discovery made twice in one year
docs.text:
In 1984, two teams announced the same breakthrough almost simultaneously. At Sumitomo Special Metals in Japan, Masato Sagawa and colleagues produced fully dense sintered Nd–Fe–B magnets from pressed powder.1 At General Motors in the United States, John Croat's group made magnets from rapidly quenched (melt-spun) ribbons.2

Both routes led to the same compound: Nd2Fe14B. Four decades later, these two processing families still dominate the industry.3

docs.title: What makes a magnet "permanent"?
docs.text:
All ferromagnets can be magnetised. A permanent magnet must also resist being demagnetised. Two numbers capture this, and both come from the hysteresis loop.

A hard magnet (wide loop) keeps its magnetisation; a soft magnet (narrow loop) loses it easily.
  • Remanence (Mr): the magnetisation left when the external field is removed. This sets how strong the magnet is.
  • Coercivity (Hc): the reverse field needed to cancel the magnetisation. This sets how stubborn the magnet is.

Together they give the maximum energy product, (BH)max. It measures how much magnetic energy a magnet can deliver per unit volume. NdFeB has the highest (BH)max of any commercial magnet, so designers can use less material for the same field.34

docs.title: Inside the crystal
docs.text:
Nd2Fe14B has a tetragonal structure with 68 atoms in each unit cell.5 Each element has a job.

Simplified side view of Nd2Fe14B. Iron supplies the magnetisation; neodymium locks it along the c axis. Property of Nd2Fe14B Typical value Why it matters Saturation polarisation, Js about 1.6 T Upper limit for remanence Anisotropy field, μ0HA around 7 T Theoretical ceiling for coercivity Curie temperature, TC about 585 K (312 °C) Magnetism vanishes above this

Intrinsic values at room temperature.5

  • Iron carries most of the magnetic moment.
  • Neodymium provides strong magnetocrystalline anisotropy. The magnetisation prefers one direction, the crystal's c axis.
  • Boron stabilises the tetragonal structure.

docs.title: The coercivity gap
docs.text:
In theory, the anisotropy field sets the upper limit for coercivity. In practice, real magnets reach only a fraction of it.6 Reversal does not happen everywhere at once. It starts at weak spots, such as defective grain surfaces or magnetically coupled neighbouring grains, and then spreads.

So coercivity is a microstructure property, not just a chemistry property. Three levers matter most:64

  1. Grain size. Smaller grains reduce the number of easy nucleation sites.
  2. Grain boundaries. A thin, non-magnetic boundary layer decouples neighbouring grains.
  3. Heavy rare earths. Adding dysprosium or terbium raises anisotropy and coercivity. However, these elements are scarce and costly.

A widely adopted compromise is grain boundary diffusion. Dysprosium or terbium is applied to the surface of a finished magnet and diffused along the grain boundaries by heat treatment. It ends up concentrated in the outer shell of each grain, exactly where reversal begins. This raises coercivity while using far less heavy rare earth than adding it to the whole alloy.7

Temperature adds a further challenge. Coercivity falls quickly as a motor heats up, so high-temperature applications such as traction motors need extra margin.3

docs.title: Three ways to make an NdFeB magnet
docs.text:
Industry makes NdFeB magnets by three main routes. They trade performance against shape freedom and cost.82

Route How it is made Strengths Typical uses Sintered Fine powder aligned in a field, pressed and sintered to full density Highest (BH)max; fully dense and anisotropic EV and wind-turbine motors, industrial drives Bonded Melt-spun flakes mixed with a polymer, then moulded or pressed Complex net shapes, tight tolerances; lower energy product Small motors, sensors, electronics Hot-deformed Melt-spun powder hot-pressed, then die-upset to create alignment Very fine grains, so good coercivity with little heavy rare earth Rings and arc segments for motors

Sintered magnets account for most of the market by value, because they deliver the strongest fields.3

docs.title: The conventional sintered route, step by step
docs.text:
The conventional powder-metallurgy route for sintered NdFeB magnets.

Each step is designed to protect a fine, well-aligned microstructure.81

  1. Melting and strip casting. The alloy is melted under vacuum and poured onto a rotating, water-cooled copper wheel. Rapid cooling gives thin flakes with a fine, uniform structure and little free iron.
  2. Hydrogen decrepitation. The flakes absorb hydrogen. The grain boundary phase expands and the flakes crack into a coarse, friable powder.
  3. Jet milling. Streams of inert gas collide the particles until they are a few micrometres across. Ideally, each particle is a single crystal.
  4. Alignment and pressing. The powder is placed in a strong magnetic field. Each particle rotates so its easy axis points the same way. The powder is then pressed, locking the alignment in place.
  5. Vacuum sintering. The pressed compact is heated to roughly 1,000 to 1,100 °C. A neodymium-rich liquid forms at the grain boundaries and pulls the part to full density.
  6. Post-sinter annealing. A lower-temperature heat treatment optimises the grain boundary phase and raises coercivity.
  7. Machining. Sintered blocks are hard and brittle. They are ground, sliced and wire-cut to final shape.
  8. Coating. NdFeB corrodes easily, so magnets are plated (often nickel-copper-nickel) or coated with epoxy.
  9. Magnetising. Finally, a short, intense pulsed field magnetises the part to saturation.

Oxygen is the enemy throughout. The fine powder oxidises rapidly, and oxides consume neodymium that should be at the grain boundaries. Modern plants therefore handle powder under inert gas from milling to sintering.8

docs.title: See it made
docs.text:
MP Materials, which mines rare earths at Mountain Pass, California, explains how rare earth magnets are made.

Manufacturing processes for sintered NdFeB magnets, from magnet maker X-Mag.

docs.title: Who makes NdFeB magnets?
docs.text: Production is highly concentrated. The International Energy Agency estimates that China produced about 94% of the world's sintered permanent magnets in 2024.9 Outside China, long-established producers include TDK, Shin-Etsu Chemical and Proterial (formerly Hitachi Metals) in Japan, and VAC (Vacuumschmelze) in Germany.10

docs.title: Processing shapes performance
docs.text: Because microstructure controls coercivity, the processing route is central. Conventional sintering needs hours at high temperature, which lets grains grow. Spark plasma sintering (SPS) instead passes a pulsed electric current through the powder under pressure.11 It reaches full density in minutes. This limits grain growth, helping preserve the fine grains that coercivity depends on.

docs.title: My work
docs.text:
At The University of Queensland, I am developing an NdFeB based magnet, from design through to a working prototype. My focus is how the processing route and composition change the final magnetic performance. I use powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering to control the microstructure.

The big picture

Demand for NdFeB is rising with electric transport and renewable energy.34 Magnets that need fewer critical elements, and that keep their coercivity when hot, will help that transition scale.

docs.title: Supercapacitors: storing energy at the surface
docs.text: Batteries store a lot of energy but release it slowly. Capacitors release energy almost instantly but hold very little. Supercapacitors sit in between. They charge in seconds and survive a very large number of cycles. The secret lies in surfaces, pores and a layer of ions just a few atoms thick.

docs.title: Where supercapacitors fit
docs.text:
Energy storage devices are often compared on a Ragone plot. It shows how much energy a device stores against how quickly it can deliver that energy.1

Supercapacitors bridge the gap between conventional capacitors and batteries. Supercapacitor (EDLC) Lithium-ion battery Storage mechanism Ions adsorb at surfaces (physical) Ions enter the electrode bulk (chemical) Charge time Seconds Tens of minutes to hours Cycle life Hundreds of thousands of cycles or more Typically thousands of cycles Energy density Low High Power density Very high Moderate

Qualitative comparison based on Simon and Gogotsi1 and Burke.2

Supercapacitors suit regenerative braking, backup power, cranes, wind-turbine pitch control and grid stabilisation, where bursts of energy matter more than duration.12

docs.title: Charge stored in a double layer
docs.text:
When a voltage is applied, ions in the electrolyte move toward the oppositely charged electrode. They form a compact layer at the surface, called the electric double layer. Charge is stored electrostatically, with no chemical reaction.3

During charging, ions line up at the electrode surface; during discharge they drift back.

The capacitance follows the familiar parallel-plate relation

C = εr ε0 Ad

where A is the electrode surface area and d is the tiny charge separation. Because d is so small, the capacitance per unit area is large. So the goal is to maximise A, using porous carbons with enormous internal surface area.13

The stored energy is

E = 12 C V2

so both capacitance and operating voltage V matter. Voltage is limited by the electrolyte. Water decomposes above about 1.2 V, so commercial cells mostly use organic electrolytes, which allow around 2.7 V per cell.1

docs.title: Anatomy of a commercial cell
docs.text:
A typical cylindrical supercapacitor contains:2

  • Two carbon electrodes, each a thin coating of activated carbon on aluminium foil. The foil acts as the current collector.
  • A porous separator between them, which lets ions through but prevents short circuits.
  • An organic electrolyte, a salt dissolved in a solvent such as acetonitrile.
  • A sealed aluminium can, with terminals connected to the foils.

Activated carbon is the workhorse electrode material. It is made by carbonising a precursor, such as coconut shell, then "activating" it to open up a network of pores. This gives surface areas of roughly 1,000 to 2,000 m2 per gram.1

docs.title: How supercapacitors are made
docs.text:
The conventional manufacturing route for wound supercapacitor cells.

The process borrows heavily from lithium-ion battery manufacturing:2

  1. Activated carbon production. A biomass precursor is carbonised, then activated with steam or chemicals to create pores.
  2. Slurry mixing. Activated carbon is mixed with a conductive carbon additive and a polymer binder.
  3. Electrode coating. The slurry is coated evenly onto aluminium foil.
  4. Drying and calendering. The coating is dried, then pressed between rollers to control thickness and density.
  5. Slitting. The wide electrode roll is cut into narrow strips.
  6. Winding. Two electrode strips and two separator layers are wound into a "jelly roll".
  7. Electrolyte filling and sealing. The roll is placed in a can, dried thoroughly, filled with electrolyte and sealed. Moisture must be kept out, because water limits the voltage and shortens life.
  8. Formation and testing. Each cell is conditioned, then tested for capacitance, internal resistance and leakage current.

Step 6 in action: an automatic winding machine for cylindrical supercapacitor cells (TOB New Energy).

A general-audience explainer on supercapacitors and their applications (Undecided with Matt Ferrell).

docs.title: Who makes supercapacitors?
docs.text: Major manufacturers include Maxwell Technologies (United States), Eaton, Nippon Chemi-Con (Japan), LS Materials (South Korea) and CAP-XX (Australia).4 Skeleton Technologies, founded in Estonia, makes its own carbon from curved, atom-thin sheets and has installed manufacturing in Germany.5

docs.title: Pores and graphene
docs.text:
Surface area alone is not the full story. Chmiola and colleagues showed that carbon pores smaller than 1 nm give an unexpected rise in capacitance.6 Ions partly shed their solvent shells to enter such pores, bringing charges closer together.

Graphene, a single layer of carbon atoms, is attractive because both of its faces are exposed. Its theoretical surface area is about 2,630 m2/g.7 In practice, graphene sheets tend to restack, which hides much of that surface.

docs.title: A second mechanism: pseudocapacitance
docs.text: Some materials add fast, reversible redox reactions at or near their surface. This is called pseudocapacitance. Metal oxides and hydroxides, such as MnO2 and Ni(OH)2, can store considerably more charge this way than carbon alone.89 The trade-off is that they often conduct electrons poorly and can be less stable over many cycles.

docs.title: Hybrid electrodes
docs.text: A natural idea is to combine both mechanisms. Conductive graphene provides surface area and electron pathways. Metal oxides and hydroxides add pseudocapacitance. The graphene also helps keep the oxide particles from aggregating.9

docs.title: My work
docs.text:
For my MSc at the Bangladesh University of Engineering and Technology, I developed a ternary hybrid electrode. It combined reduced graphene oxide (rGO) with Ni(OH)2 and MnO2.10 The material formed a wrinkled, flower-like structure that improved charge storage. I have since applied machine learning to carbon supercapacitor design; see my Machine Learning page.

The big picture

Supercapacitors will not replace batteries. They complement them, handling the fast, high-power jobs that batteries do poorly. Better electrode materials can extend their energy density while keeping their speed.
